accuracy.evidence: Checked for the past tense in young children's talk: regular past adds -ed (jumped, played, kicked, walked) and common irregular verbs change (go/went, eat/ate, run/ran, see/saw) in standard English; DfE Development Matters 2021 Reception Communication and Language and the EYFS ELG Speaking (past, present and future tenses); over-regularisation (goed, runned) as a normal stage after the -ed rule is learned (Marcus et al. 1992); recasting as the advised adult response (Saxton 2005; Speech and Language UK). The adult text says will + verb is one common way to talk about the future, not the only one, and the lab only uses clear time cues (yesterday, last night, I am ... now, I will ...).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented over-regularisations goed, eated, runned and seed (step 3 options, robot sentences, challenge tags), the over-correction slip of 'fixing' a right regular verb once irregulars are learned (two robot sentences are already right and prediction 3 asks about 'jumped'), and time-word mismatches such as 'Yesterday I will go' and 'Tomorrow I saw' (step 5 and challenge feedback).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagpasttalk is built on this topic's own mechanism: a yesterday/today/tomorrow sort of spoken sentences, an -ed machine where a dragged -ed tile visibly joins the word, an irregular-past finder where the regular-looking 'goed' option is answered with 'go is a word that changes', a robot whose sentences are judged right or fixed, and time-word frames that need went, will go or saw. Gate: under 30% shingle overlap with every other flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child discovers by doing: -ed visibly joins four regular words, so the rule is seen; the same rule then fails for go, eat, run and see, with feedback naming the changed word; the robot step makes them decide when -ed is right as well as when it is wrong; the frames show the time word deciding the form. Done messages confirm each idea in one plain line.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'jump' for yesterday (the -ed machine), 'goed' (step 3, where goed is rejected), and 'jumped is wrong too' (the robot step, where it is right). Each step's done message reveals the locked-in prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven questions, each wrong option tagged to its own slip with its own message: goed, eated, runned, seed (a plant word, and tomorrow needs will see), saw for tomorrow, will for yesterday, a present-tense form for the past, kicken (-ed not -en) and jamp (jump just adds -ed).

readability.evidence: Family lesson for ages 4 to 5: kid text in very short sentences of common words ('Go, went. Eat, ate.'), within the learn/readability.py limit, adult text within its limit. Canvas text is one sentence or one word per card at 16 to 28 px; every step can be done by a grown-up reading aloud.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate passes (no filler phrases, under 12% overlap with any lesson). Each kid paragraph teaches one point (what yesterday is, -ed, words that change, time words); the adult paragraphs give the curriculum link, the regular and irregular rule, why goed happens and how to respond, named mistakes and a lab summary.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark: the sentence card and three day boxes are large, the -ed tile is 110 by 70 px, the word options in step 3 are full-width 64 px cards, the robot's Right and Fix it buttons span half the width each, and the three frame words sit in one row with readable 18 px text. Young class gives 56 px buttons under the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button: Yesterday, Today now and Tomorrow labelled with the sentence, Add -ed labelled with the word, one button per option labelled 'Yesterday I went', Right and Fix it labelled with the robot's sentence, and one button per frame word labelled with the whole sentence. say() updates the canvas aria-label and a polite live region after every action; the walk gate's axe run is clean (WCAG 2.1 AA) in both themes on desktop and iPhone.
